name: Femi Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal day on site like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am Femi Weber, 58, a junior worker fitting doors and helping with framing at a block of flats. I left school early, came here after a warehouse closed, and still ask the joiner to check a difficult hinge. The work gives me pride, but carrying frames up three floors makes my shoulders ache.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one troubles me most because it leaves very little time to get steadier wages before the 2031 robots. Paid supervised training and actual local vacancies would help; a list of courses without jobs would not.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who teaches an older beginner when the skilled joiner is rushed. That is how I learn, and if he loses time to new targets, my mistakes become more expensive.

headlineQuote: You did not ask who teaches an older beginner when the skilled joiner is rushed.
portrait: Femi is a **58-year-old junior** construction worker who entered the trade after his warehouse closed.
He uses AI **occasionally**, adopting a tool after a skilled colleague proves it on a real delivery.
His **thin savings** and Nessa’s variable market takings leave rent and roof repairs exposed to lost shifts.
He seeks **supervised training** and paid openings, while admitting that robots could eventually reach those jobs too.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** gives Femi little time to secure wages before robots can do his site tasks around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **paid supervised training** and real local vacancies for older beginners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the lads at the flats site that clever quotes on a phone do not hang a door straight. I sometimes use the AI question box to check a material name, but I still ask the joiner before ordering anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I am not relaxed just because the machines disappoint. I am 58, still a junior hand after changing trades, and my partner Nessa and I have less than a month of bills saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking the same paid site shifts and keep my notebook of measurements beside the tool bag. In the first year I would put ten from any full-pay Friday into a separate rent envelope, if the grocery bill leaves it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel familiar with the work and uneasy about the money. A quiet year for AI could still be a bad year for our roof repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What brought you into building work this late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I left school early and worked at a warehouse until it closed; a neighbour taught me enough to get on this crew. I am proud to be learning, though a faster joiner still checks my hinges.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when a week of shifts is lost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nessa sells at a market stall, and bad weather can cut her takings too. We would postpone the roofer and pay the rent first, because our grown children have expenses of their own.

say: I would say **AI answers** cannot hang a door straight.
I would tell the crew I still check **material names** with an experienced joiner.
think: My **junior wages** and thin savings make ordinary site stoppages frightening.
I do not expect a **quiet AI year** to fix the leaking roof.
do: Keep taking **paid site shifts** and recording measurements in my notebook.
Put **ten** from full-pay Fridays into a rent envelope when groceries allow.
feel: **Familiar** with the work, but uneasy about household bills.
S0.quote: A quiet year for AI could still be a bad year for our roof repairs.
fieldNote: Femi treats the AI question box as an **occasional reference**, while deferring actual orders to a skilled joiner.
The old **roof leak** and variable market takings explain anxiety even when the technology changes little.

steps.text: Keep taking paid shifts at the flats site and record measurements
Put ten from full-pay Fridays into a rent envelope when possible

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the software might buy materials quicker, but someone should check what arrives before it is fixed to a wall. I would ask the contractor to show us a working tool before making everybody use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the office can plan and price faster, the boss may demand more doors hung in a day. I am slower than the qualified men, so a tighter contract might cost me a shift long before a robot touches a drill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the joiner to demonstrate the delivery-checking app on the next order and practise it after the shift. In the first year I would still hang doors for pay, and ask my cousin who repairs bicycles whether he needs Saturday help if our site hours fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel watchful rather than excited. Once I see a tool work twice, I will use it; I will not stake my wages on a sales pitch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would convince you the app is useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the app caught a wrong door size before we carried it up three floors, that would count. I would write the result in my notebook and try it again, not just take the office word.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much could Saturday work matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bicycle shop could cover a few food bills, not replace construction pay. I would rather stay with the crew, but a Saturday paid by the job is better than an empty week.

say: I would say **deliveries** still need a worker to check them.
I would ask for a **real demonstration** before the contractor changes our routine.
think: I fear **faster planning** could bring targets I cannot meet as a junior.
A lost **site shift** matters more than a clever ordering screen.
do: Practise the **delivery-checking app** after a joiner demonstrates it.
Keep hanging **doors for pay** during the first year.
Ask my **bicycle-repair cousin** for Saturday work if site hours fall.
feel: **Watchful** about targets and willing to try a proven tool.
S1.quote: Once I see a tool work twice, I will use it; I will not stake my wages on a sales pitch.
fieldNote: Femi accepts new technology when a **specific delivery error** proves its value, matching his measured approach to change.
His proposed **Saturday repair work** supplements rather than replaces the site wage, and depends on reduced hours.

steps.text: Practise the delivery-checking AI app after a joiner demonstrates it
Keep hanging doors for pay in the first year
Ask his bicycle-repair cousin for Saturday work if site hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that 2028 changes the drawings and orders, while hands still build for roughly three years. I would want the contractor to tell us what the robot trial means for wages before asking for volunteers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 60 when the thinking work changes, and cheap plans could reduce the office staff or squeeze our prices. At 63 in 2031, a robot that can hang doors as well as us could erase the junior tasks I have only just learned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my paid shifts now and ask the supervisor for a written record of the door and framing jobs I have completed. In 2029 I would apply for the occasional building caretaker opening at the school, and keep working on site while I wait; in 2031 I would ask my cousin about full-time bicycle repairs if the robots take the doors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel a jolt of fear, especially when I think of the rent. I believe work should be earned, but it is hard to earn a shift when the machine can do the whole task.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could school caretaker work survive the machines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I cannot know whether the school would replace a caretaker too, so the application is a bridge, not a promise. I would still put it in while a real vacancy exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your grown children for money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask our children for help only if we were about to lose the flat. They have jobs and their own bills; I would first ask my cousin whether the bicycle bench had room.

say: I would tell the crew **thinking AI** arrives before capable site robots.
I would ask for **clear wages** before joining any robot trial.
think: At **60**, cheap planning may squeeze our contractor and my paid hours.
At **63**, capable robots could take the junior door work I depend on.
do: Keep **paid site shifts** and request a written record of completed jobs.
Apply for a **school caretaker** vacancy in 2029 while remaining on site.
Ask about **full-time bicycle repairs** if robots take the door work.
feel: **Afraid** for rent, yet intent on finding paid work.
S2.quote: I believe work should be earned, but it is hard to earn a shift when the machine can do the whole task.
fieldNote: Femi links the **2028 office change** to possible wage pressure, then the 2031 robots to direct loss of site tasks.
The **caretaker application** is explicitly uncertain; he does not claim either maintenance or bicycle repair is robot-proof.

steps.text: Keep taking paid door and framing shifts through 2029
Apply for a school caretaker opening in 2029
Ask cousin about bicycle repair work in 2031 if robots replace door-fitting
Ask grown children for help only if losing the flat becomes imminent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years is long enough for an employer to teach people what changes at the site. I would ask for an apprenticeship place for older beginners as well as school leavers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 63 in 2031, AI may do all the plans while I still need wages from fixing their mistakes in real rooms. At 66 in 2034, the robots could also fix the rooms; I cannot count a pension I have never checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask our trade association now about a short, paid course in measuring and fitting accessible doorways, and enroll if there is a funded place. In 2032 I would keep site shifts and apply for repair work at the housing cooperative; before 2034 I would sit with Nessa and write down what we actually need each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel some room to prepare and a nagging fear that the course could lead nowhere. Five years lets me try an apprenticeship, but it does not guarantee anyone will hire a 66-year-old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why accessible doorways?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We fitted one wider doorway last month, and I liked getting the clearance right for a neighbour using a chair. I still needed the joiner to check the frame, which is why I want proper supervised training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your monthly list change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The list would tell Nessa and me whether the market stall plus my remaining hours could cover rent, food and the roof. I do not want to announce retirement on a guess.

say: I would ask for **older beginners** to have a fair shot at paid apprenticeships.
I would say **five years** gives employers time to teach before site work changes.
think: At **63**, planning AI could leave me fixing mistakes in physical rooms.
At **66**, capable robots could do those repairs while my pension remains unknown.
do: Enroll in a **funded doorway course** if the trade association offers one.
Apply for **housing cooperative** repair work in 2032 while taking site shifts.
List **monthly rent and food** costs with Nessa before 2034.
feel: **Hopeful** about a training place, yet fearful it may not lead to wages.
S3.quote: I do not want to announce retirement on a guess.
fieldNote: Femi chooses **supervised doorway training** after a real fitting job revealed a skill gap, but enrollment depends on funding.
He keeps **paid site work** central and wants a monthly budget before making claims about retirement.

steps.text: Enroll in funded accessible-doorway training if offered by the trade association
Apply for housing cooperative repair work in 2032
Keep taking paid site shifts during 2032

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a decade gives the contractor time to replace people fairly, not simply stop calling them in. I would ask the association to publish how many older hands still get paid site days each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 in 2036, I may already be taking lighter tasks because my shoulders complain after lifting frames. At 71 in 2039, robots could take those tasks too, and our rent will still arrive unless we have moved or saved enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep site work while my shoulders allow it and put a small fixed amount from each complete week toward the roof and rent cushion. In 2037 I would ask the housing cooperative about paid inspection visits, and check with Nessa whether a smaller flat would cost less after moving fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel less rushed but not safe. A decade is useful only if we use the wages while they are there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would inspection visits be a safe retirement job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the thinking system may already do the report and a robot could later make the visit. I would apply if the cooperative actually had openings, but I would not build retirement around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a move worthwhile?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a smaller flat saved enough rent after the deposit and van, Nessa and I would move near the market where she sells. Our grown children could visit us there, but they should not have to finance it.

say: I would ask the association for **paid-day figures** for older site workers.
I would say contractors have **ten years** to make changes fairly.
think: At **68**, shoulder pain may reduce my site work before AI changes planning.
At **71**, robots may remove remaining tasks while rent still needs paying.
do: Keep **site work** while my shoulders allow it.
Build a **roof and rent cushion** from complete weeks.
Apply for **cooperative inspection visits** in 2037 if vacancies exist.
feel: **Less rushed**, though rent remains an open worry.
S4.quote: A decade is useful only if we use the wages while they are there.
fieldNote: Femi sees **physical strain** as a nearer risk than thinking AI under the longest timeline.
He treats inspection as **paid work to pursue**, not a guaranteed refuge from advanced AI or robots.

steps.text: Keep taking site work while his shoulders allow it in 2037
Put a fixed amount from complete weeks toward roof and rent savings
Apply for cooperative inspection visits if vacancies exist in 2037
Move near Nessa’s market if net rent savings cover moving costs
